paragraphs: What came next was close to an orgy, a feast where everyone was welcome. Grushenka was the first to ask for wine.
“I want a drink. I want to get properly drunk, the way we did before. Do you remember, Mitya? Do you remember how we made friends here last time?”
Mitya was nearly delirious himself. He felt his happiness was within reach. But Grushenka kept sending him away from her side.

“Go and enjoy yourself. Tell them to dance and have a good time, ‘let the stove and cottage dance,’ just as we had it last time,” she kept calling. She was tremendously excited, and Mitya hurried to do as she said. The chorus was waiting in the next room. The room where the two of them had been sitting was too small. Cotton curtains split it in two, and behind them stood a huge bed with a puffy feather mattress and a pile of cotton pillows stacked like a pyramid. The four guest rooms all had beds in them. Grushenka sat down right by the door, and Mitya set an easy chair for her. She had sat in that same spot “the time before” to watch the dancing and singing, when they had made merry there. All the girls who had come tonight had been there then. The Jewish band with fiddles and zithers had come too, and in the end the long-awaited cart had turned up with the wines and provisions.

Mitya rushed about. All sorts of people began drifting into the room to watch. They were peasants and their women, woken from sleep and drawn by the hope of another wonderful entertainment like the one they had enjoyed a month earlier. Mitya remembered their faces and greeted and hugged everyone he knew. He uncorked bottles and poured wine for whoever came up. Only the girls were really eager for the champagne. The men liked rum and brandy better, and hot punch best of all. Mitya had chocolate made for all the girls. He also ordered three samovars kept boiling all night, so that anyone could help himself to tea and punch.

What followed was an absurd, chaotic muddle, but Mitya was in his element, and the sillier it got, the higher his spirits climbed. If the peasants had asked him for money just then, he would have pulled out his notes and given them away by the handful. That was probably why the landlord, Trifon Borissovitch, kept hovering near Mitya to protect him. He seemed to have given up all thought of bed that night. Still, he drank very little, just one glass of punch, and in his own fashion he kept a sharp eye on Mitya’s interests. He stepped in at just the right moment and, civil and fawning, talked Mitya out of giving the peasants “cigars and Rhine wine,” and above all money, as he had done the time before. He was also very indignant to see the peasant girls drinking liqueur and eating sweets.
“They’re a lousy lot, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” he said. “I’d kick every last one of them, and they’d take it as an honor. That’s all they’re worth!”

Mitya thought of Andrey again and had punch sent out to him. “I was rude to him just now,” he said again, in a sinking, softened voice. Kalganov didn’t want to drink and at first didn’t care for the girls’ singing. But after a couple of glasses of champagne he turned extraordinarily lively. He strolled around the room, laughing, praising the music and the songs, admiring everybody and everything. Maximov, blissfully drunk, never left his side. Grushenka was starting to get drunk too. She pointed at Kalganov and said to Mitya:
“What a dear, charming boy he is!”

And Mitya, delighted, ran to kiss Kalganov and Maximov. Oh, his hopes were high! She still hadn’t said anything, and she seemed to be holding back on purpose. But now and then she looked at him with tender, passionate eyes. Finally she suddenly seized his hand and pulled him hard toward her. At that moment she was sitting in the low chair by the door.
“Why did you come in just now, eh? You simply walked in!... I was scared. So you wanted to hand me over to him, did you? Did you really want that?”
“I didn’t want to get in the way of your happiness!” Mitya stammered, blissful. But she didn’t need his answer.
“Well, go and have a good time ...” she sent him off again. “Don’t cry. I’ll call you back.”

So he ran off, and she listened to the singing and watched the dancing, though her eyes followed him wherever he went. A quarter of an hour later she would call him again, and once more he would come running.
“Come here, sit by me and tell me. How did you find out about me, and about my coming here yesterday? Who did you hear it from first?”
And Mitya started to tell her everything, in a disjointed, rambling, feverish way. He spoke oddly, frowning often and breaking off suddenly.
“What are you frowning about?” she asked.
“Nothing.... I left a man lying ill back there. I’d give ten years of my life to see him get better, to know he was all right!”

“Oh, forget him, if he’s ill. So you were going to shoot yourself tomorrow! What a silly boy! Why? I like reckless men like you,” she lisped, her tongue a little unsteady. “So you’d go to any lengths for me, would you? Were you really going to shoot yourself tomorrow, you fool? No, wait a bit. Tomorrow I might have something to tell you.... I won’t say it today, but tomorrow. You’d like it to be today? No, I don’t feel like it today. Now go on, go and amuse yourself.”
Once, though, she called him over, puzzled and anxious.

“Why are you sad? I can see you’re sad.... Yes, I can see it,” she added, looking hard into his eyes. “You keep kissing the peasants and shouting, but I can tell something’s wrong. No, be merry. I’m merry, so you be merry too.... There’s somebody here I love. Guess who. Ah, look, my boy has fallen asleep, the poor dear. He’s drunk.”

She meant Kalganov. He was indeed drunk and had dozed off for a moment, sitting on the sofa. But it wasn’t only the drink that made him sleepy. He had suddenly sunk into gloom, or, as he put it, “boredom.” The girls’ songs depressed him deeply, because as the drinking went on they gradually turned coarse and wilder. The dances were just as bad. Two girls were dressed up as bears. A lively girl named Stepanida, stick in hand, played their keeper and started to “show them off.”
“Look sharp, Marya, or you’ll get the stick!”
In the end the bears rolled on the ground in the most indecent way, to roars of laughter from the crowd of men and women packed around them.
“Well, let them! Let them!” said Grushenka gravely, a rapturous look on her face. “When they get a day to enjoy themselves, why shouldn’t folks be happy?”
Kalganov looked as if someone had thrown mud on him.
“It’s disgusting, all this peasant silliness,” he muttered, moving away. “It’s what they play at in summer, when it never gets dark.”
There was one “new” song, set to a jaunty dance tune, that he disliked in particular. It told of a gentleman who came to try his luck with the girls and see whether they would love him:
The master came to try the girls: Would they love him, or would they not?
But the girls could not love the master:
He would beat me cruelly, And such love is not for me.
Then a gypsy comes along and tries his luck as well:
The gypsy came to try the girls: Would they love him, or would they not?
But they couldn’t love the gypsy either:
He’d be a thief, I fear, And cause me many a tear.
And many more men come to try their luck, a soldier among them:
The soldier came to try the girls: Would they love him, or would they not?
But the soldier is turned down with scorn, in two indecent lines. They were sung with perfect frankness and set the audience roaring. The song ends with a merchant:
The merchant came to try the girls: Would they love him, or would they not?
And it seems he wins their love, because:
The merchant will make gold for me, And his queen I’ll gladly be.
Kalganov was truly indignant.

“That’s only a song from yesterday,” he said aloud. “Who writes this stuff for them? They might just as well have had a railwayman or a Jew come to try his luck with the girls. He’d have won them all.”

And, almost as if he had been personally insulted, he announced right there that he was bored. He sat down on the sofa and fell asleep at once. His pretty little face looked rather pale as his head fell back on the cushion.
“Look how pretty he is,” said Grushenka, leading Mitya over to him. “I was combing his hair a while ago. It’s like flax, and so thick....”
And, bending over him tenderly, she kissed his forehead. Kalganov opened his eyes at once and looked at her. Then he got up and asked, very anxiously, where Maximov was.
“So it’s him you’re after.” Grushenka laughed. “Stay here with me a minute. Mitya, go and find his Maximov for him.”

As it turned out, Maximov couldn’t tear himself away from the girls. He only ran off now and then to pour himself a glass of liqueur. He had drunk two cups of chocolate already. His face was red, his nose crimson, and his eyes moist and sickly sweet. He came running up and announced that he was going to dance the “sabotière.”
“They taught me all those well-bred, aristocratic dances when I was little....”
“Go with him, Mitya, go on. I’ll watch from here how he dances,” said Grushenka.

“No, no, I’ll come and watch too,” cried Kalganov, brushing aside, quite innocently, Grushenka’s offer to sit with him. They all went to watch. Maximov danced his dance. But nobody much admired it except Mitya. It was nothing but skipping and hopping, with kicks of the legs, and at every skip Maximov slapped the sole of his raised foot. Kalganov didn’t like it at all, but Mitya kissed the dancer.
“Thank you. Are you tired, maybe? What are you looking for? Want some sweets? Or a cigar?”
“A cigarette.”
“Wouldn’t you like a drink?”
“Just a liqueur.... Do you have any chocolates?”
“Yes, there’s a heap of them on the table over there. Pick one, my dear soul!”
“I like the vanilla kind ... for old people. Hee hee!”
“No, brother, we don’t have that special kind.”
“I say,” the old man leaned over to whisper in Mitya’s ear. “That girl there, little Marya, hee hee! What if you helped me get friendly with her?”
“So that’s what you’re after! No, brother, that won’t do!”
“I wouldn’t do anyone any harm,” Maximov muttered, crestfallen.
“Oh, fine, fine. But they only come here to dance and sing, you know, brother. Damn it all, just wait!... Meanwhile, eat, drink and enjoy yourself. Don’t you want some money?”
“Later, perhaps,” Maximov smiled.
“All right, all right....”

Mitya’s head was burning. He went out onto the wooden balcony that ran along the inner side of the whole building, above the courtyard. The fresh air revived him. He stood alone in a dark corner, and suddenly he clutched his head in both hands. His scattered thoughts came together. His feelings merged into one, and it threw a sudden light into his mind. A fearful, terrible light! “If I’m going to shoot myself, why not now?” The thought went through him. “Why not fetch the pistols, bring them here, and finish it here, in this dark, filthy corner?” For almost a minute he stood undecided. A few hours earlier, as he raced here, he had been pursued by disgrace, by the theft he had committed, and by that blood, that blood!... Even so, it had been easier for him then. Then everything was over. He had lost her and given her up. She was gone, as far as he was concerned. Oh, then his death sentence had been easier to bear. At least it had seemed necessary and unavoidable, for what was there to keep him on earth?

But now? Was it the same as then? Now at least one phantom, one terror, was over. That first, rightful lover, that fateful figure, had vanished without a trace. The terrible phantom had shrunk into something so small and so comic. It had been carried into the bedroom and locked in. It would never come back. She was ashamed, and from her eyes he could now tell who it was she loved. Now he had everything he needed to be happy in life ... and yet he could not go on living, he could not. Oh, damnation! “O God! Bring back to life the man I knocked down at the fence! Let this fearful cup pass from me! Lord, You have worked miracles for sinners like me! But what, what if the old man is alive? Oh, then I would wipe out the shame of the other disgrace. I would give back the stolen money. I’d return it, I’d find it somehow.... Not a trace of that shame will be left, except in my heart forever! But no, no. Oh, these are impossible, cowardly dreams! Oh, damnation!”

And yet a ray of light and hope shone in his darkness. He sprang up and ran back to the room, to her, to her, his queen forever! Was one moment of her love not worth all the rest of life, even with the agonies of disgrace? This wild question gripped his heart. “To her, to her alone, to see her, to hear her, to think of nothing, to forget everything, if only for tonight, for an hour, for a moment!” Just as he turned from the balcony into the passage, he ran into the landlord, Trifon Borissovitch. The man looked gloomy and worried, he thought, and he imagined he had come looking for him.
“What is it, Trifon Borissovitch? Are you looking for me?”
“No, sir.” The landlord seemed thrown off balance. “Why would I be looking for you? Where have you been?”
“Why are you so glum? You’re not angry, are you? Wait a bit, you’ll be in bed soon.... What time is it?”
“Three o’clock, I’d say. Past three, it must be.”
“We’ll stop soon. We’ll stop.”
“Please, don’t mention it, it makes no difference. Keep it up as long as you like....”

“What’s wrong with him?” Mitya wondered for a moment, and ran back to the room where the girls were dancing. But she wasn’t there. She wasn’t in the blue room either, where only Kalganov lay asleep on the sofa. Mitya looked behind the curtain, and there she was. She was sitting in the corner on a trunk, bent forward, her head and arms resting on the bed beside her. She was crying bitterly, trying with all her might to smother her sobs so that no one would hear. When she saw Mitya she beckoned to him, and as he ran to her she gripped his hand tight.

“Mitya, Mitya, I loved him, you know. How I’ve loved him all these five years, all that time! Did I love him, or only my own anger? No, him, him! It’s a lie that it was my anger I loved and not him. Mitya, I was only seventeen then. He was so kind to me, so cheerful. He used to sing to me.... Or that’s how it seemed to a silly girl like me.... And now, O Lord, he’s not the same man. Even his face isn’t the same. He’s completely different. I wouldn’t have known him. I drove here with Timofey, and all the way I kept wondering how I’d meet him, what I’d say to him, how we’d look at each other. My soul was faint, and then all at once it was as if he had thrown a bucket of dirty water over me. He talked to me like a schoolmaster, so grave and learned. He received me so solemnly that I was struck dumb. I couldn’t get a word in. At first I thought he was ashamed to talk in front of his great big Pole. I sat staring at him and wondering why I couldn’t say a word to him now. It must have been his wife who ruined him. You know he dropped me to get married. She must have changed him like that. Mitya, how shameful it is! Oh, Mitya, I’m ashamed, I’m ashamed for the rest of my life. Curse it, curse it, curse those five years!”
